claims.text: Conventional casting produces porosity in CoCrFeNiTi.
As-cast CoCrFeNiTi has a homogeneous, soft, single-phase FCC structure.
High-energy ball milling induces severe plastic deformation and atomic mixing.
Rapid sintering after milling will suppress porosity in CoCrFeNiTi.
Controlling displacement rate during sintering will minimize stresses and cracking caused by thermal-expansion mismatch between FCC and BCC phases.
The range 900–1050 °C is below the Ti-induced HCP nucleation threshold in CoCrFeNiTi.
Rapid heating and cooling constitute a high sintering strain rate that limits the diffusion time available for HCP formation.
Fast cooling can kinetically inhibit HCP nucleation in the proposed CoCrFeNiTi process.
The high defect density produced by milling hinders the FCC-to-HCP transition.
Milling raises dislocation density and reduces grain size, thereby increasing the driving force for solid-solution formation.
Rapid sintering supplies enough diffusion for FCC homogenization while remaining too short for HCP nucleation.
Rapid cooling prevents brittle intermetallic and HCP phase formation.
A high strain rate during sintering enhances particle bonding and suppresses porosity without excessive grain growth.
The proposed process will produce a dense, nanocrystalline solid solution dominated by FCC with a minor BCC fraction.
The processed alloy will be more than 20% harder than the as-cast alloy because of grain refinement and solid-solution strengthening.
Avoiding HCP and Laves phases will avoid the brittleness associated with those phases.
Excessive sintering temperature or slow cooling will allow HCP formation and cause brittleness.
Oxygen or carbon impurities during sintering may stabilize HCP and confound phase selection.
Nanoindentation at 10 mN with a 10 s dwell time is proposed to measure hardness and elastic modulus.
The hypothesis is declared falsified if HCP exceeds 5 vol.% or hardness fails to increase by more than 20% relative to the as-cast baseline.

contradictions.description: The structural mediator says kinetic hindrance suppresses the thermodynamic drive toward HCP, whereas the mechanism describes the thermodynamic tendency as remaining present but inaccessible because nucleation is too slow. Kinetic hindrance suppresses transformation, not the thermodynamic driving force.

The conditions confidently designate 900–1050 °C as below the CoCrFeNiTi HCP threshold, while the uncertainty field states that the relevant temperature window is not characterized by the cited evidence.

The predicted hardness is attributed jointly to grain refinement and solid-solution strengthening, but the falsification rule treats a hardness increase alone as evidence for grain-refinement hardening and does not separate the two contributions.
